title: Tulkus
hookLine: teachers recognized as rebirths of earlier masters

lines: A CHILD REACHES FOR THE TEACHER'S.
cards: A few visitors arrive at a farmhouse, dressed plainly. On a table they set down some objects in pairs: two rosaries, two walking sticks, two small drums.

One of each pair belonged to a teacher who died some years before; the other is a look-alike. A small child toddles over, studies them, and reaches, without much fuss, for the ones that were the teacher's.
The visitors glance at each other. Scenes like this are told in the stories of how a tulku is found. It isn't the whole process, and it isn't proof on its own.
But it is how a search can end.

teach.b: Tulku is the Tibetan word used to translate the Sanskrit nirmanakaya, the emanation body: the form in which awakened mind appears in the world.
In everyday Tibetan use, a tulku is a teacher recognized as the rebirth of an earlier master. In Buddhist teaching, beings are ordinarily carried into rebirth by their karma.
A tulku is understood differently: a teacher who, out of compassion, chooses to return, to carry on the work with the same students and the same monastery.
The Dalai Lamas and the Karmapas are both lines of this kind, each one recognized as the return of the one before. How is one found?

Tradition describes several signs, and searchers weigh them together: a letter the teacher left about where to look, the dreams and visions of senior lamas, omens around a birth, and finally the child, tested with things that were the teacher's.

Then a recognition is announced, and the child is raised and educated in the monastery. Tibetan teachers speak about the hard part openly. Recognitions have sometimes been disputed, and politics has sometimes pressed in.
And teachers are clear that a title is a beginning, not a finish line: a recognized tulku still has to study for years, take vows, practice, and earn the trust of students like anyone else.
What the system holds onto is a thread: a teacher, a monastery, a community of students, and the hope that the one who cared for them has returned.

how: In Tibetan Buddhism, when certain teachers die, senior lamas search for their rebirth using letters, dreams, signs and tests with the teacher's belongings; a recognized child, called a tulku, is then raised and educated in the monastery.

o: a family heirloom handed down to the eldest child
a young monk chosen by lot to lead a monastery
a teacher recognized as the return of an earlier master

p: the child picks the teacher's things

s: once recognized, a tulku needs no training
a tulku still has to study for years, take vows and practice like anyone else.
letters, dreams and visions, omens, and the child's response to the teacher's belongings.

games.q: you're part of a search party. a small child in front of you has just reached for the old teacher's rosary, not the copy. what happens next?
o: the child is crowned and starts teaching tomorrow.
it's weighed with the other signs, and if recognized, the child is raised and educated in the monastery.
nothing: the test is just for fun.
games.why: the test is one sign among several. a recognized child begins years of study: a title is a beginning, not a finish line.

practice: If something came down to you from an older generation, a ring, a book, a recipe card, hold it in your hands; if not, rest your hands on your knees and think of one thing you know how to do that came down that way.
Let the line run backward, who had it before you, and before them, a chain of hands longer than you can see. Then let a quiet thank-you travel down the whole length of it.

wordCard.voice: Tulku. The emanation body: in Tibet, a teacher recognized as the return of an earlier master, who must still study and practice. Today's word.

orig.note: Tibetan sprul sku: sprul, emanation, and sku, body. It renders the Sanskrit nirmanakaya.

carryVoice: Your line: returned. A title is only the place where the long work begins. Until tomorrow.
